blocks.content: A function is the smallest unit of design in any codebase. It is even smaller than a class or module, but the quality of a codebase is often decided by the quality of its functions.

Good functions are easy to read, easy to understand, and easy to change. They do one thing, have names that clearly express their purpose, accept only the parameters they truly need, and either perform an action or return information never both at the same time.

blocks.content: 1. Do One Thing Rule
The most important rule of function design is simple: a function should do one thing.

The challenge is that almost any function can be described as doing one thing if the description is vague enough. For example, saying "this function handles an order" sounds like a single responsibility, but inside it may validate data, calculate taxes, save records, and send emails. Those are multiple responsibilities hidden behind a broad description.
A practical way to identify this problem is the one-sentence test. Try describing the function in a single sentence without using the word "and".
Good: Four functions, one job each
["Calculate the total price of an order.","Validate a user's login credentials.","Send a password reset email."]
items: Calculate the total price of an order.
Validate a user's login credentials.
Send a password reset email.

blocks.content: Bad: One function, four jobs
["Validate the order and calculate tax.","Save the order and send a confirmation email.","Fetch user data and update the dashboard."]
items: Validate the order and calculate tax.
Save the order and send a confirmation email.
Fetch user data and update the dashboard.

blocks.content: If the description naturally requires "and", the function is likely doing more than one thing and should be split into smaller functions.

Smaller functions are easier to understand, easier to test, and safer to modify. When a bug appears or a requirement changes, there is only one place to look and one responsibility to update. That's what makes code remain maintainable as the system grows.
2. The Parameter Problem
Every parameter a function accepts is something the caller must provide correctly. The more parameters a function has, the easier it becomes to make mistakes.
With one or two parameters, mistakes are rare. But as the list grows, callers must remember what each parameter means and the exact order in which they should appear.
Consider this function:
createUser(name, email, city, country, isAdmin, sendWelcome)

codes.cpp: createUser(name, email, city, country, isAdmin, sendWelcome)
codes.javascript: createUser(name, email, city, country, isAdmin, sendWelcome)

blocks.content: A caller might write:

createUser(
    "Ana",
    "a@x.com",
    "Canada",
    "Toronto",
    false,
    true
);
The code compiles. The program runs. No error is reported. But there is a bug. The city and country values were swapped. The system now stores:
["City = Canada","Country = Toronto"]
items: City = Canada
Country = Toronto

blocks.content: This is the most dangerous kind of bug because nothing crashes. Everything appears to work, but the data is wrong.

Long parameter lists also make function calls difficult to read. When someone sees six or seven values in a row, they often need to jump to the function definition to understand what each value represents.

A good function minimizes this burden. If a function needs many parameters, it's often a sign that related values should be grouped into an object instead. Shorter parameter lists make functions easier to call, easier to read, and much harder to misuse.
Fixing It with a Parameter Object
blocks.text: Fixing It with a Parameter Object

blocks.content: A common solution to long parameter lists is to group related values into a single object, often called a parameter object.
Instead of passing many values separately, the caller creates one object that contains all the required information. This makes the function signature shorter and the code easier to understand.
createUser(name, email, city, country, isAdmin, sendWelcome);

The code compiles, but city and country are swapped. After introducing a parameter object:

codes.python:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UserRegistration:
    name: str
    email: str
    city: str
    country: str
    is_admin: bool
    send_welcome: bool


class UserService:
    def create_user(self, registration: UserRegistration) -> None:
        print(f"Creating user: {registration.name}, {registration.email}, "
              f"city={registration.city}, country={registration.country}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    registration = UserRegistration(
        name="Ana",
        email="a@x.com",
        city="Toronto",
        country="Canada",
        is_admin=False,
        send_welcome=True,
    )

    UserService().create_user(registration)

blocks.content: Now the function accepts a single object instead of six separate values.

codes.python:
class UserRegistration:
    def __init__(self, name, email, city, country, is_admin, send_welcome):
        self.name = name
        self.email = email
        self.city = city
        self.country = country
        self.is_admin = is_admin
        self.send_welcome = send_welcome

    def create_user(self):
        print(f"Registered {self.name} in {self.city}, {self.country}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    registration = UserRegistration(
        name="Ana",
        email="a@x.com",
        city="Toronto",
        country="Canada",
        is_admin=False,
        send_welcome=True,
    )

    registration.create_user()

blocks.content: This approach provides two major benefits.

["First, the function signature becomes cleaner and easier to read. 
","Second, all user-related information is grouped together in one place, making the code easier to maintain as the application grows.
"]
items: First, the function signature becomes cleaner and easier to read.
Second, all user-related information is grouped together in one place, making the code easier to maintain as the application grows.

blocks.content: As a general rule, when a function starts accumulating many related parameters, consider creating a parameter object. It reduces complexity for callers and makes the intent of the code much clearer.
3. Commands vs Queries
Functions generally fall into two categories: commands and queries.

["A query answers a question without changing anything. Calling it multiple times is safe because it only reads data.
","A command performs an action and changes state. Its purpose is to do something, not answer questions.
"]
items: A query answers a question without changing anything. Calling it multiple times is safe because it only reads data.
A command performs an action and changes state. Its purpose is to do something, not answer questions.

blocks.content: Problems begin when a single function does both. A function that changes state while also returning information creates hidden side effects. The caller may think it's simply asking a question, while the function is quietly modifying data underneath.
A good rule is simple:
["Commands should change state and return nothing.","Queries should return information and change nothing."]
items: Commands should change state and return nothing.
Queries should return information and change nothing.

blocks.content: Keeping these responsibilities separate makes code easier to understand, easier to test, and far more predictable. When reading a function call, developers should immediately know whether it is performing an action or simply providing information.

Step 2: The caller invokes popAndCheck().
Step 3: The function removes the first item from the queue.
Step 4: The function checks whether the queue is empty.
Step 5: The function returns the answer.
Step 6: The caller invokes popAndCheck() again expecting similar behavior.
Step 7: The function removes another item from the queue.
Step 8: The function checks whether the queue is empty again.
Step 9: The answer is different because the first call already changed the queue.
Step 10: The caller gets different results from the same function because it both changed state and answered a question.

blocks.content: This is the problem with mixing a command (remove an item) and a query (check if empty) in the same function.
MIXED: a single method both mutates AND returns information about the result

codes.python:
from collections import deque


class TaskQueue:
    def __init__(self):
        self.tasks = deque()

    def add_task(self, task):
        self.tasks.append(task)

    def pop_and_check(self):
        self.tasks.popleft()          # command - mutates state
        return len(self.tasks) == 0   # query - answers a question


if __name__ == "__main__":
    queue = TaskQueue()
    queue.add_task("task-1")
    queue.add_task("task-2")

    empty_after_first_pop = queue.pop_and_check()
    print(f"Empty after first pop: {empty_after_first_pop}")

    empty_after_second_pop = queue.pop_and_check()
    print(f"Empty after second pop: {empty_after_second_pop}")

blocks.content: SEPARATED: two small functions, each doing exactly one of the two jobs
CALLER: explicit about which is happening at each step

queue.pop();
if (queue.isEmpty()) { /* react to empty state */ }
blocks.code:
queue.pop();
if (queue.isEmpty()) { /* react to empty state */ }

codes.javascript:
queue.pop();
if (queue.isEmpty()) { /* react to empty state */ }

blocks.content: Python's list.pop() is a common exception to this rule. It both removes an item from the list and returns that item.
This is generally accepted because the name pop clearly tells developers that the list will be modified and a value will be returned.

The lesson is not that mixed functions are always bad. The lesson is that if a function both changes state and returns a value, its name should make that behavior completely obvious. Such functions should be rare exceptions, not the normal way of writing code.
4. Function Length and the Extract Method Habit
blocks.text: 4. Function Length and the Extract Method Habit

blocks.content: There is no fixed rule for how long a function should be. A function is probably too long when it starts doing multiple things or needs comments to explain different sections.
A comment is often a function waiting to be created: If you write a comment like:
// Validate input
it usually means that block can become a function called validateInput().
The main function should read like a list of steps: A good function should be easy to scan and understand. Reading it should feel like reading the steps of a process, not the implementation details.

blocks.content: The goal is simple: short, focused functions that are easy to read and understand.
5. Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Generic Function Names
Functions like processOrder(), handleRequest(), or doStuff() are often too vague.
A vague name is usually a sign that the function is doing multiple things. If a function cannot be described with a clear, specific name, consider splitting it into smaller functions.
Mistake 2: Boolean Flag Parameters
A function like save(order, sendEmail) changes its behavior based on a boolean value.
This often means two separate responsibilities are hiding inside one function. Separate functions usually make the code clearer and easier to understand.
Mistake 3: Hidden Side Effects
blocks.text: Mistake 3: Hidden Side Effects

blocks.content: A function named getBalance() should only return the balance.
If it also updates a cache, reconnects to a database, or modifies state, callers get unexpected behavior because the name suggests a simple query.
Mistake 4: Too Many Same-Type Parameters
blocks.text: Mistake 4: Too Many Same-Type Parameters

blocks.content: When a function accepts several strings or numbers in a row, it's easy to pass them in the wrong order.
The code still runs, but the result may be incorrect. Grouping related values into an object helps prevent these mistakes.
6. Quick Reference

["Do One Thing: A function should have one responsibility. If you need the word \"and\" to describe it, it's probably doing more than one thing.
","Keep Parameters Small: Two or three parameters are easy to understand. If the list becomes long, use a parameter object.
","Avoid Same-Type Parameters: Multiple strings or numbers can be swapped accidentally. Use named fields or parameter objects to make mistakes harder.
","Separate Commands and Queries: A function should either change state or answer a question. Avoid functions that do both.
","Comments Often Reveal Missing Functions: If a code block needs a comment to explain it, that block may deserve its own function.
","Generic Names Are a Warning Sign: If you can't give a function a clear and specific name, it's often because the function is trying to do too much."]
items: Do One Thing: A function should have one responsibility. If you need the word "and" to describe it, it's probably doing more than one thing.
Keep Parameters Small: Two or three parameters are easy to understand. If the list becomes long, use a parameter object.
Avoid Same-Type Parameters: Multiple strings or numbers can be swapped accidentally. Use named fields or parameter objects to make mistakes harder.
Separate Commands and Queries: A function should either change state or answer a question. Avoid functions that do both.
Comments Often Reveal Missing Functions: If a code block needs a comment to explain it, that block may deserve its own function.
Generic Names Are a Warning Sign: If you can't give a function a clear and specific name, it's often because the function is trying to do too much.
